subject: zoology
question_text: What is trinomial nomenclature? Give an example.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.49, VSAQ 62). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. ADDED BEYOND THE BOOK: the second example (Corvus splendens splendens) is standard and is not printed in this book's answer, which gives Homo sapiens sapiens only.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: What trinomial naming is
steps.why: Binomial naming has two words and stops at the species, so a third word is added only when a named subspecies has to be shown.
common_mistakes: Writing only two words. Two words is binomial naming; trinomial naming has three.
Putting the subspecies name first. The order is genus, species, subspecies.
steps.memory_tip: Tri means three: genus, species, subspecies — in that order.
steps.margin_note: One sentence naming the three words in order, then the example.

steps.label: The example
steps.why: Writing the three parts of the name against the three ranks proves that the third word is the subspecies and not a repeat.
common_mistakes: Giving a two-word name as the example. The example must have three words.
Underlining only part of the name. All three words are written in italics, or each is underlined separately.
steps.memory_tip: Homo sapiens sapiens: the last word repeats, and that repeat is the subspecies.
steps.margin_note: One example is enough. Say which word is which.
